desc:
A well-formed parentheses string is primitive if it is non-empty and cannot be split into two non-empty well-formed strings. Every well-formed string s splits in exactly one way into a sequence of primitive strings placed side by side. For example "(()())(())" splits into "(()())" and "(())".

Remove the outermost pair of parentheses from every primitive piece and glue the remains together in the original order. For the example above you get "()()" and "()", so the answer is "()()()".

Return the resulting string, which is empty if every piece was just "()".
hints: The outermost parentheses are exactly the ones that sit at the top level, where nothing else is open yet.
Track the current depth. A '(' read at depth 0 starts a primitive piece, and a ')' that brings the depth back to 0 ends it.
Keep a character only if it is not one of those two: add '(' when the depth before it is at least 1, and add ')' when the depth after it is at least 1.
editorial: The outermost pair of a primitive piece is the opening bracket where the depth goes from 0 to 1 and the closing bracket where it goes back from 1 to 0. Everything strictly between them is kept. So one pass with a depth counter is enough, without any explicit stack.

For each character: if it is '(', keep it when the depth is already above 0, then increase the depth. If it is ')', decrease the depth first and keep it when the depth is still above 0. Time is O(n) and the output takes O(n) space.
